Each measure is the mean of pupil_z (participant z-score of the cleaned pupil size) in a window after an event, minus the mean of the 200 ms before that event (subtractive baseline). Blinks and tracking loss are removed with a margin, and gaps up to 500 ms are interpolated in the preprocessing. A window value is used when at most 25 % of its bins are missing after interpolation and the baseline is complete; otherwise only that measure is missing for the trial.

Bite and blocked attack with a net on the attack slot

With at least one net on the attack slot, whether the mosquito gets through is random (pass probability .5 with one net, .29 with two, .15 with three). There are 5,948 such trials with an attack: 2,217 bites and 3,731 blocked attacks, from 85 participants. Without the post-rating trials within the task

Leaving out only the first trial of the session (83 trials with a baseline, 0.6 %) reduces the three couplings about as much as leaving out all post-pause trials. On the first trial the model’s state uncertainty is at its maximum: +3.4 SD of the within-participant deviation on average, where 1.2 % of the other trials exceed ±3 SD. The cue baseline is +1.9 z above the participant mean, after the rating screen and before any task experience. These trials contribute 42 % of the within-participant cross-product of baseline and state uncertainty. The pooled within-participant slope (in z per SD) is 0.091 with them and 0.057 without them.

No transition trial follows a pause, so the regular trials, the reference of the contrast, contain all post-pause trials with their raised baselines. Leaving out the post-rating trials within the task or the post-break trials each reduces the contrast; leaving out both gives −0.10.
Score moderation of the update coupling.

The post-rating trials within the task change it most (general factor −2.00° → −1.71°); the first trial and the post-break trials change it little. The pause covariates leave it unchanged, because they shift the level of these trials, not their slope. In a model on all regular trials with the interaction attack pupil × score × post-pause trial (8,522 trials, 516 of them after a pause; random intercept), the general-factor moderation is −1.68° (p = .009) in the trials without a pause, with a further −5.76° (p = .024) in the trials after a pause. In these trials the attack pupil is measured relative to a raised cue-period level, and the next update toward the attack is larger (+4.7° after a rating screen within the task, relative to the participant mean).

Relation to the working reading of the behaviour

children.label: Relation to the working reading of the behaviour

children.value: The working reading of the behaviour has two parts:

Higher scores go with relying more on internal structural representations to interpret new evidence, and with attributing surprising outcomes to noise until they are confirmed. This would help under structural ambiguity (Partial Instructions).
With explicit structure (Full Instructions), higher scorers may build larger hypothesis spaces, try to track all rules and reduce irreducible uncertainty, and end up more uncertain and slower.
The behavioural signs are higher noise reactivity in the λ variant of the model, splitting at t+2, and less following of transitions at t+1. Against this reading, the pupil results are:

In the attack window, the coupling with surprise is near 0 and does not change with the general factor or any scale. In the feedback window, the coupling with surprise and with the belief update is larger with a higher general factor (q < .001 and q = .021) and with higher STICSA scores. For the general factor this is clearest in Full Instructions (feedback ~ surprise +0.060, q = .018), but the conditions do not differ; for STICSA trait it is present in all three conditions. A smaller response to surprise with higher scores is not seen in either window.

With a higher general factor, the update toward the attack goes less with the attack pupil (−1.64° per SD, q = .027; IU, OCI and STICSA trait in the same direction, q ≤ .043). With lower scores a larger attack pupil goes with a slightly larger update; with higher scores, with a smaller one. This is in the direction of discounting outcomes that evoke a larger response. Part of this moderation is carried by the trials after a rating screen (see
Updating after a bite that is pure noise.

With a net on the attack slot, a bite is a random outcome. After such a bite the next placement moves toward the attack in None (+3.6°) and Partial (+5.8°, q = .057), but not in Full (−0.2°; Full vs None + Partial −5.0°, p = .15). This pattern fits a reading in which explicit instructions let participants attribute the bite to the stochastic barrier rule (aleatoric uncertainty), while without them the bite is treated as possibly informative about the attack direction (epistemic uncertainty); the condition difference does not pass the tests here. With higher IU scores the shift after an unlucky bite is smaller (−3.4° per SD, p = .031, q = .062). The general factor does not change the shift (−0.9°, p = .52), in no condition.
Pupil, model and scores within the conditions

higher scores go with a cue baseline that follows the model’s state uncertainty more closely than in Full, and (STICSA trait) with a baseline that declines more steeply over the trials of an episode. Across participants, a larger feedback response to surprise goes with higher stable-trial accuracy, most clearly in Partial. This pattern is in the direction of the first part of the reading (structure used where it has to be inferred).

higher scores go with a larger feedback response to surprise and to the belief update (general factor), with no decline of the baseline over the episode; the oddball tracking of the feedback pupil does not change with the scores. This is weakly in the direction of the second part; the feedback moderation is not specific to Full.

the ISI pupil does not follow the state uncertainty more strongly with higher scores in Full. The signature “surprise registered but attributed to noise” is not seen either: a larger feedback response to surprise goes with lower noise reactivity in the adopted model (r = −0.23, q = .062), not with a higher one.
The ISI pupil, the last window before the attack is known, is larger with a higher general factor (+0.073 z per SD, q = .015), STICSA state and OCI, in None and Partial.
